questions.q: Why does ordinary least squares regression tend to struggle with typical financial factor features?
options: Financial features are always categorical
Features are often noisy and collinear (overlapping), producing large, unstable coefficients
OLS cannot handle more than one feature at a time
Financial data is always perfectly stationary
questions.explain: Engineered financial factors (e.g., multiple momentum windows) often overlap heavily in the information they capture, which makes OLS coefficients unstable and sensitive to small data changes.

questions.q: What does Ridge regression (L2 penalty) do to model coefficients?
options: It sets most coefficients to exactly zero
It shrinks coefficients toward zero but rarely sets any to exactly zero
It has no effect on coefficients at all
It only affects the intercept term
questions.explain: Ridge penalizes the sum of squared coefficients, shrinking them toward zero to reduce variance, but it generally keeps all of them nonzero.

questions.q: What distinguishes Lasso regression (L1 penalty) from Ridge?
options: Lasso can push some coefficients to exactly zero, effectively performing feature selection
Lasso never changes any coefficients
Lasso requires unscaled features
Lasso can only be used for classification, not regression
questions.explain: Lasso's L1 penalty can drive some coefficients to exactly zero, which amounts to automatic feature selection -- something Ridge's L2 penalty typically does not do.

questions.q: Why is feature standardization important before fitting Ridge, Lasso, or Elastic Net?
options: It is not actually necessary for any of these models
These models penalize coefficient magnitude directly, so features need to be on comparable scales for the penalty to be applied fairly
Standardization is only needed for neural networks
It converts the regression into a classification problem
questions.explain: Because Ridge/Lasso/Elastic Net penalize coefficient size, a feature on a much larger scale would be penalized disproportionately unless all features are first standardized.

questions.q: What does Elastic Net do, and why is it often a practical choice for financial factor sets?
options: It removes the need for any regularization
It blends the L1 and L2 penalties, getting some of Lasso's feature selection while keeping more of Ridge's stability under collinearity
It only works with decision trees
It is identical to ordinary least squares
questions.explain: Elastic Net's `l1_ratio` mixes L1 and L2 penalties, balancing Lasso's feature selection against Ridge's stability -- useful for the overlapping, noisy feature sets common in finance.
